title: Cathie Wood Picks a Side Between Palantir and Google
detail:
Cathie Wood Picks a Side Between Palantir and Google
Moz Farooque ACCA

PLTR
GOOG

Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Cathie Wood made a notable shift inside ARK Invest's AI portfolio Tuesday, buying roughly $11.2 million of Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) while selling about $3.5 million of Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL).

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Sign with PLTR.

Is PLTR fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

PLTR GF Value chart

ARK purchased 63,638 Palantir shares on Nov. 3 after the stock slipped 1.65% despite reporting another strong quarter. At the same time, the firm sold 12,530 Alphabet shares, taking some money off the table after Google's parent had fallen nearly 14% since its earnings release.

The contrast is interesting because both companies are delivering strong AI growth, but investors are questioning very different things.

Palantir reported 96% year-over-year revenue growth, with Q3 sales reaching $2.31 billion versus the $2.17 billion analysts expected. Adjusted EPS of $0.44 also beat the $0.40 consensus. U.S. commercial revenue surged 148% to $984 million, overtaking domestic government revenue for the first time.

Still, investors remain uneasy about valuation and future contract growth. Total contract value increased only 6%, while U.S. commercial contract value grew 11%, raising questions over whether Palantir can maintain its current pace.

Alphabet's problem is different.

Its Q3 revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion, while Google Cloud more than doubled to $30.71 billion. But advertising revenue missed expectations, and the company's enormous AI infrastructure buildout pushed quarterly free cash flow to negative $9.1 billion. Alphabet expects 2026 capex of $195 billion to $205 billion, with spending set to rise again in 2027.

Interestingly, Wall Street is currently more bullish on Alphabet. TipRanks shows an average Alphabet price target implying roughly 43% upside, versus about 30% for Palantir.

Investor takeaway

I think the important point is that Wood is not simply choosing AI over something else.

She is rotating within AI.

Palantir offers explosive software growth and much lower capital intensity, but at a very demanding valuation. Alphabet trades at a more conventional multiple, but investors are increasingly questioning how much cash its AI infrastructure will consume before the returns become obvious.

That makes the trade revealing.

ARK appears more willing to add to Palantir's valuation risk than Alphabet's capex risk right now.

For investors, the key things to watch are Palantir's contract growth and valuation, Alphabet's free cash flow and capex, and whether ARK continues building PLTR while trimming GOOGL.

Cathie Wood, head of Ark Investment Management, often sees falling stock prices as an opportunity to add to her favorite technology investments.

Sometimes, she buys shares on the way down, hoping to pick them up at a bargain. That's what she did this week with Palantir Technologies (PLTR), adding shares after the AI software company's stock dropped following its third-quarter earnings report.

Last year, her flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Wood's flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is up 4.45% as of writing, while the S&P 500 surged 12.63%, Yahoo Finance data shows.

Wood gained a reputation after the Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Nov. 3, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -8.26%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 10.18% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar.

Cathie Wood remains optimistic about AI and tech revolution

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott. That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking. 

Wood defended her investment strategy after an audience member at a recent summit questioned ARK's performance compared with the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ).

Related: Cathie Wood buys $9.1 million of tumbling tech stock

"Investors deserve to understand both their returns and the decisions behind them," Wood said in a post on X on Oct. 5.

She argued that the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and QQQ are built differently. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, while ARK actively invests in companies it believes are driving disruptive innovation across industries including healthcare, financial services and transportation.

Wood has long been optimistic about AI, which she sees as a major driver of productivity, economic growth, and corporate profits in the years ahead. She has also pushed back against fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

The 2026 midterm results are in, and the Democrats won in a landslide. So what does this mean for Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) stock? Maybe nothing good, but also maybe... nothing.

Shares of the artificial intelligence and defense contractor sold off more than 6% in early trading, before paring their losses to just 1% as of 11:15 a.m. ET Wednesday. And yet, Wall Street's reaction to the sea change in government seems muted -- or even positive in Palantir's case.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Bad news for defense contractors?

President Donald Trump had requested $1.5 trillion for fiscal year 2027 defense spending in the months leading up to November's election. A Democratic Congress may not approve anything like that.

At last report, the U.S. Senate will number 54 Democrat votes to just 44 Republicans, and the House of Representatives is tilting blue 228-139 (with 68 seats unconfirmed). Even before the results are all in, Politico reports the Pentagon plans to reduce its spending request from $1.5 trillion to $1.1 trillion. With more than half its revenue coming from government contracts, many military, this could be bad news for Palantir.

What's next for Palantir stock

And yet, Wall Street seems unconcerned. This morning, Barclays analyst Anthony Valentini raised his target price on Palantir to $273 with an overweight rating, reports StreetInsider.com. Bank of America's Mariana Perez Mora reiterated her buy rating on Palantir, too, with a $255 price target implying 47% upside.

Why? "Palantir can no longer be viewed only as a government services/software provider with its commercial growth engine running hot," says Mora. While its government sales grew 78% year-to-date, Palantir's commercial sales year-to-date roughly doubled.

Assuming it can pivot to emphasize its commercial business and keep growing at this rate, Palantir stock should do just fine.

We just published the list of the 10 Best Meme Stocks to Invest In and Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) ranked 7th on this list.

Nobody has to double their money every year to build real wealth. An investor who puts $10,000 into a stock that returns 15% annually and holds it for 40 years ends up with about $2.7 million. That takes patience, not a lucky guess.

Reaching for stocks that promise to multiply overnight makes that outcome less likely, not more, because a single collapse can wipe out years of compounding. That tension is the subject of our look at whether Sandisk can keep climbing after a 1,322% gain in a year.

Hedge funds work from the opposite instinct. On average, they don't load up on lottery-ticket stocks. They back companies they judge most likely to deliver higher returns for an amount of risk they can live with.

Photo by Arturo Añez on Unsplash

Bubble Warnings Spread as Retail Traders Pull Back

Veteran voices are urging care. Yahoo Finance reported on October 9 that Bridgewater Associates' Ray Dalio said the market is close to bubble territory. Panmure Liberum head market strategist Joachim Klement expects the AI bubble to burst in either 2027 or 2028, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Bank of America Securities' Jill Carey Hall wrote in a client note that retail clients were net buyers, the first retail inflows since late July.

Everyday traders have cooled off since then. Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider wrote in a note that retail trading volumes have fallen about 20% since mid-summer, and retail made up 9% of US equity volume, near its lowest level since 2020, according to Yahoo Finance on October 26. You might also be interested in reading our piece on whether Palantir can justify a multiple five times its sector's.

The speculative money has not gone quiet, though. Snider's note showed retail trading in leveraged index funds running at roughly double the pace of ordinary funds tracking the same indexes, and Robinhood data pointed to retail options trading nearly doubling over the past year.

Palantir chief executive Alex Karp said demand for AI sovereignty has been unleashed, and the second-quarter numbers gave him plenty to point to. Revenue rose 93% from a year earlier to $1.935 billion. US commercial sales grew 149%, to $764 million, and the value of US commercial contracts signed in the quarter was a record at $2.132 billion, up 153%.

Profits kept pace with sales. Adjusted operating margin reached 62%, up from 46% a year earlier. Palantir raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $8.150 billion and $8.158 billion, and it lifted its outlook for adjusted operating income and free cash flow too. The new free cash flow range is $4.5 billion to $4.7 billion.

title: Palantir’s Revenue Grew 96%. Its New Contract Value Grew 6%. Alex Karp Explains Why
detail:
Palantir’s Revenue Grew 96%. Its New Contract Value Grew 6%. Alex Karp Explains Why
Roxanna Maglangit

PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Palantir's Revenue Grew 96%. Its New Contract Value Grew 6%. Alex Karp Explains Why ©@iJeab via Canva, @nuttapong punna from nuttapong punna's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Palantir fell 3% today even though third-quarter revenue grew 96% to $2.31 billion, because total contract value grew just 6% to $2.92 billion.

CEO Alex Karp says commercial customers are signing shorter contracts that start much bigger and grow fast, so less contract value gets booked at the start.

Commercial contract value grew 17% and U.S. commercial customers grew 29%, but U.S. commercial remaining deal value rose only 4% from the second quarter.

The stock is priced for years of fast growth, so the next two quarters' bookings need to show those shorter contracts growing the way Karp says they will.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) just had its first $2 billion quarter. Revenue of $2.31 billion grew 96% and beat the $2.18 billion analysts expected going in. Adjusted EPS of $0.44 topped the $0.41 expected, and management raised its guidance again.

The stock fell 3% today anyway.

Investors focused on a different number: total contract value (TCV), the full value of the deals Palantir signed in the quarter. It came to $2.92 billion, up just 6% from a year ago.

Today's contracts are tomorrow's revenue

Revenue counts what Palantir earns on contracts it has already signed. TCV counts what it signs now, which becomes revenue over the months and years ahead.

The slowdown came fast. Contract value grew 61% in the first quarter and 49% in the second, when Palantir booked $3.37 billion. U.S. commercial TCV hit a record $2.13 billion in the second quarter. This time it came in at $1.46 billion, up 11%.

That matters for a stock priced for years of fast growth. Going into the report, analysts expected revenue to climb from $4.48 billion in 2025 to $17.89 billion in 2028:

Palantir Technologies (PLTR): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Palantir's new 2026 guide of $8.53 billion, up 91%, already beats the $8.22 billion consensus, so I'd expect those estimates to rise. But the later years depend on contracts Palantir still has to sign.

TIKR tracks 32 analysts on Palantir. How many say "Buy"?

Karp's answer: shorter deals, much bigger starts

On the Nov. 2 call, CEO Alex Karp said that on the front line in commercial, he's seeing "much quicker interaction, much quicker to deployment, shorter duration of the contract, but then an ability to expand that contract dramatically."

The first deals are also far bigger than they used to be: "So instead of being, like, $250,000, it's like $25 million to start."
